events.reason: Right flank pain radiating to groin with nausea

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
reports.text: Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis, renal stone protocol. A 4 mm calculus is present at the right ureterovesical junction with mild right hydronephrosis and hydroureter proximal to it. Left kidney normal without hydronephrosis. No other urinary tract calculi. Appendix normal. Liver, spleen, pancreas and adrenal glands unremarkable on this noncontrast exam. Uterus and adnexa unremarkable. No free fluid.
reports.conclusion: 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild right hydronephrosis.

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth daily until the stone passes, up to 4 weeks
Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain, with food
Dissolve 1 tablet on the tongue every 8 hours as needed for nausea

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Service date 2025-02-18 — copy to PCP

Chief complaint: right flank pain.

31-year-old woman with a history of kidney stones (two prior episodes) woke around 11 pm with sudden severe pain in the right flank, now 6 hours, wrapping around to the right groin. Nauseated, has not vomited. No fever. No burning, frequency or visible blood in the urine. Does not think she could be pregnant. Also has mild persistent asthma; treated for pulmonary TB in 2023, completed.

Meds: albuterol inhaler prn. Allergies: dust mites, pollen. No drug allergies.
Never smoker, no alcohol.

Afebrile. BP 130/85, HR 95.
Writhing, cannot get comfortable, clearly in a lot of pain. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft without peritoneal signs. Right CVA tenderness.

UA: SG 1.015, pH 5.5, RBC 10-15/hpf, WBC 2-3/hpf, no bacteria, nitrite negative, no casts or crystals.
Urine hCG: negative.
CT A/P without contrast: 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild right hydronephrosis.

ED course: IV ketorolac and IV ondansetron with good relief. Tolerating PO.

Assessment: right ureterolithiasis, uncomplicated (no sign of infection, pain controlled).
Plan: discharge. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily until passage (up to 4 weeks), ibuprofen 600 mg q6h prn, ondansetron 4 mg ODT prn. Strain all urine and keep the stone. Push fluids. Follow up with PCP this week; urology if not passed in 2-4 weeks. Return for fever, uncontrolled pain or vomiting.

orders.reason: Recurrent nephrolithiasis, third episode; right UVJ stone

documents.title: Phone Call — ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Called after ED record came in (2/18, 4 mm R UVJ stone, mild hydro, UA without infection). Pain much better, using ibuprofen twice a day, no nausea since yesterday, no fever. On tamsulosin, a little lightheaded standing up, ok if she gets up slowly. Straining urine.

Third stone: placing urology referral so they can look at prevention. Bring the stone in when it passes and we'll send it for analysis. Call for fever, chills, vomiting or pain not controlled.

documents.title: Stone!
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good news, I passed it yesterday afternoon and caught it in the strainer. It's tiny! No pain since. Should I keep taking the tamsulosin? And where do I bring the stone?

documents.title: RE: Stone!
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Great news! Dr says you can stop the tamsulosin now. Drop the stone off at the front desk in a clean dry container (no tissue) any time today and we'll send it to the lab for analysis. Keep the urology appointment, they'll want to talk about prevention.

documents.title: Stone analysis result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your stone was calcium oxalate, which is the most common kind. The urologist will go over prevention with you on the 26th; mostly it comes down to plenty of fluids and watching salt.

documents.title: Urology Consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 2025-03-26
Referring: primary care. Thank you for this referral.

HPI: 31F with a third stone episode. ED 2/18 with right renal colic; CT showed a 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild hydronephrosis. Passed spontaneously 2/23 on tamsulosin, captured. Two prior episodes, both passed without intervention. Asymptomatic now. Father with recurrent stones.

Meds: albuterol prn. NKDA.

Exam: well, no CVA tenderness.

Data: stone analysis calcium oxalate monohydrate. CT images reviewed: no residual stones on either side.

Impression: recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, currently stone free.

Recommendations:
- Fluids to make at least 2.5 L of urine a day; aim for at least 2.5-3 L intake, more on running days and in summer.
- Moderate sodium.
- Keep normal dietary calcium; do not cut out dairy.
- No medication at this time.
- Return or call with new symptoms. Follow up as needed.

documents.title: Albuterol refill
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, last refill on my albuterol. Pollen has been rough this spring, used it a little more in May (maybe once or twice a week), better now.

documents.title: RE: Albuterol refill
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Renewed. Let's look at your asthma together at the physical in September. If you're needing it more than twice a week again before then, message me.

documents.title: Annual Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
32F here for yearly visit.

Interval: kidney stone in February (4 mm R UVJ, passed, calcium oxalate). Saw urology in March: fluids, moderate salt, normal calcium, no meds. She now carries a 1 L bottle and refills it 3 times a day. No stone symptoms since.
Asthma: spring was the worst it's been in a while, 1-2x/week albuterol in May, now back to a few times a month. No night symptoms, no ED.
Hx TB 2023, treated. No cough, fever, sweats.
Still in the PhD program and working in the lab. Running 3-4x/wk. No alcohol. PHQ-2 0.

Exam: Well. Lungs clear, no wheeze. Heart RRR. Abd soft, no CVA tenderness. Skin normal.

A/P
1. Mild persistent asthma — albuterol prn.
2. Recurrent nephrolithiasis, calcium oxalate — hydration per urology; BMP and UA today.
3. Allergic rhinitis due to pollen.
4. Personal history of TB.
5. HM: Pap 2024 normal co-test, next 2029. Flu/COVID next month. 
RTC 1 year.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Kidney function, calcium and the urine test are all normal. Keep up the water bottle routine.

documents.title: Nurse Visit — Vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Seasonal flu and 2025-26 COVID vaccines given, one in each arm. No reactions with prior doses, feeling well. Observed, no issues.

events.reason: Cough, fever and fatigue for 10 days

reports.text: PA and lateral chest. Bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates. No lobar consolidation. No pleural effusion. No cavitation. Heart size normal.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates, compatible with atypical pneumonia.

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (500 mg) by mouth on day 1, then 1 tablet (250 mg) daily on days 2 through 5

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
ED PHYSICIAN NOTE (DOS 2/5/2026) — forwarded to primary care

CC: cough and fever x 10 days

32-year-old woman with mild persistent asthma and recurrent kidney stones (ED last year for a right ureteral stone; ED in 2022 for an asthma flare). Pulmonary TB treated to completion in 2023. Ten days of dry cough, low-grade fevers and fatigue. It began with a sore throat; the last week she has had mild headaches. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no blood in sputum. No night sweats or weight loss. She lives in shared graduate housing and several of her housemates have had the same kind of illness in the past couple of weeks. She came back in mid-January from a winter-break trip to an area where malaria is present.

Meds: albuterol prn. Allergies: dust mites, pollen; NKDA. Never smoker.

T 38.1 C (100.6 F), HR 90, RR 18, BP 120/78.
Alert, not toxic. Oropharynx clear. Lungs: scattered crackles at both bases, no wheezing. Heart regular. No rash.

Rapid flu A/B negative. CBC: WBC 7.9, lymphocytes 46%. Malaria smear negative.
CXR: bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates.

Impression: atypical pneumonia, most likely Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila or Legionella given the cluster among housemates and the gradual course. Picture and timing do not suggest TB reactivation (no sweats or weight loss, interstitial not upper-lobe pattern, sick contacts), and malaria smear is negative. Outpatient treatment appropriate.

Plan: azithromycin 500 mg today then 250 mg daily x 4 days. Fluids and rest. Albuterol if wheezy. PCP follow-up within a week; return for shortness of breath, chest pain, high fever or if not improving in 48-72 hours.

orders.reason: Follow-up of pneumonia, history of treated TB

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED 2/5 with atypical pneumonia (bilateral interstitial infiltrates, flu neg, malaria smear neg), on azithro, last dose tomorrow. ED note reviewed.

No fever since Saturday. Cough still there but less, not keeping her up. Energy maybe 70%. Headaches gone. Needed albuterol twice over the weekend for chest tightness with coughing fits, none since. No sweats, appetite fine.

Exam: Looks well. Afebrile, sat normal. A few fine crackles at the bases, no wheeze. Heart RRR.

A/P
Atypical CAP improving. Finish azithro. Cough can linger for weeks. Given her TB history, I'd like a repeat film in about 6 weeks to make sure it's cleared; ordered. Albuterol prn. Call if fever returns, breathing worsens, or sweats/weight loss.
